chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Fadalah ibn Ayyub, from Umar ibn Aban, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the Imams (peace be upon them both), who said:
I asked him about nabidh (fermented drink) whose boiling had settled/stopped. He said, 'He said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon Him and His Family) said: Every intoxicant is forbidden.'

And I asked him about theظروف (containers/vessels). He said, 'The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon Him and His Family) forbade the dubba' (gourd vessel), the muzaffat (pitched vessel), and you added the huntam (pottery vessel), meaning the ghadar (clay pot). And the muzaffat means the zif (pitch/resin) which is in the ziq (skin vessel) and is poured into the khawab (jars) to make it better for the wine.'
And I asked him about the green jars and the lead-lined ones. He said, 'There is no harm in them.'

key_terms.الدُّبَّاء: Al-Dubba': A vessel made from a dried gourd.
key_terms.اَلْجِرَار: Al-Jirar: Large earthenware jars or pots.
key_terms.اَلْحَنْتَم: Al-Hantam: A type of pottery vessel.
key_terms.اَلْمُزَفَّت: Al-Muzaffat: A vessel coated with pitch/resin.
key_terms.مُسْكِر: Muskir: Intoxicant; that which causes intoxication.
key_terms.نَبِيذ: Nabidh: A fermented drink made by soaking dates or raisins in water.

ai.seo_question: What are the rulings on nabidh and the containers used for wine in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib* details the Prophet’s prohibition of all intoxicants and specific pre-Islamic wine vessels (dubba, muzaffat, huntam), while permitting green and lead-lined jars. It highlights the Shia jurisprudential focus on both the substance (kullu muskirin haram) and the material context of consumption, linking ritual purity to practical storage methods.
